title: Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness

contents: Humans versus Econs: the predictable biases real people bring to choices
Choice architecture: there is no neutral design — every menu, form, and default steers
Libertarian paternalism: steer toward welfare while preserving freedom to opt out
Defaults at work: automatic pension enrolment, Save More Tomorrow, organ-donation regimes
Money, health, and freedom: applications from mortgages and Medicare to the environment
The Final Edition's additions: sludge — friction engineered against the chooser — and smart disclosure

audiences: Product and UX people who set defaults for a living
Readers of Thinking, Fast and Slow wanting the applied sequel
Anyone auditing how their own choices get framed

sources.title: Nudge (book)
sources.supports: Publication history (Yale UP 2008; Final Edition 2021), the choice-architecture and libertarian-paternalism framework, the policy influence including nudge units, Thaler's 2017 Nobel, and the documented criticisms from Neuberger, Gigerenzer, and Kolbert.

sources.title: Nudge: The Final Edition
sources.supports: Final Edition bibliographic record: Penguin Books, 2021-08-03, 384pp, ISBN 9780143137009.

sources.title: The effectiveness of nudging: A meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions across behavioral domains
sources.supports: The field-wide meta-analysis of over 200 choice-architecture studies reporting a small-to-medium average effect — the strongest quantitative case that nudging works on average.
sources.limitations: Averages across heterogeneous interventions; contested by the publication-bias reply.

sources.title: No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias
sources.supports: The documented rebuttal: after correcting the same corpus for publication bias, the average nudge effect is statistically indistinguishable from zero — the sharpest modern challenge to the book's empirical foundation, while domain-specific effects (notably defaults) remain more robust.
sources.limitations: A bias-correction result, itself methodologically debated; does not test any single intervention.

sources.title: On the supposed evidence for libertarian paternalism (as documented in the reception record)
sources.supports: The heuristics researcher's documented critique: the nudge label has stretched until 'almost everything that affects behavior has been renamed a nudge', and the programme underrates teaching people to decide (boosting) versus steering them.
sources.limitations: Accessed via documented quotation; Gigerenzer is the rival school's champion.

sources.title: Review of Nudge (as documented in the reception record)
sources.supports: The paternalism objection in its documented form: if choosers cannot recognise their own interests, 'why stop at a nudge? Why not offer a push, or perhaps even a shove?'

sources.title: Nudge
sources.supports: Large, durable reception: praised as the applied behavioural-economics primer; recurring complaints that the second half reads as policy-wonk case lists.

workflow.coverage_notes: Built from the documented record, both sides of the peer-reviewed effectiveness debate, the named critiques, and reader reception.
